pr_title: Add attributes to statistics with binary_sensor source
pr_body:

Previously, `unit_of_measurement` was not set on `statistics` sensors that would measure a `binary_sensor` input. The `unit_of_measurement` will now be stet to `changes` to reflect the count this sensor measures.

Add knowable attributes to `statistics` sensor when it is used for a `binary_sensor`. In particular set `unit_of_measurement` attribute to `value` so the count is treated as a number rather than a state that happens to be a number.

@fabaff - feel free to push back on this. I'm not sure if making the support for `binary_sensor` more robust is in your vision of the `statistics` sensor. I started using the counting behavior and I was hoping to make life easier for people doing the same thing in the future but I can also understand if it makes the sensor more complicated and you'd rather deprecate that behavior.

Even if the complexity to support `min_age` and `max_age` is not desired I'd be happy to trim this just to publishing `sampling_size`, `count` and `unit_of_measurement` which are much safer and would be in keeping with how this sensor behaves when it's operating on a standard numeric input.
We should probably mark the changed unit of measurement as a breaking change. Please add a breaking change paragraph to the PR description.

> @fabaff - feel free to push back on this. I'm not sure if making the support for binary_sensor more robust is in your vision of the statistics sensor. I started using the counting behavior and I was hoping to make life easier for people doing the same thing in the future but I can also understand if it makes the sensor more complicated and you'd rather deprecate that behavior.

Nowadays the `counter` integration could cover the use-case that is part here for the `binary_sensor`. Still the counting of the state changes in this integration is super simple (doesn't require to use a service). Thus, no argument against to make it more robust.

> Even if the complexity to support min_age and max_age is not desired I'd be happy to trim this just to publishing sampling_size, count and unit_of_measurement which are much safer and would be in keeping with how this sensor behaves when it's operating on a standard numeric input.

Covering the aging make sense as it could be relevant and improves the integration from a "simple counter" to more "statistical relevance".

To your point about counter and how this is different: the age-out behavior of this sensor is pretty convenient compared to the `counter` integration. For instance, I have a bouncy motion sensor so having a 5-minute interval of `statistics` can allow me to differentiate a room being occupied from someone passing through.

issue_context.title: Statistics Sensor has no attributes when measuring `binary_sensor` entities
issue_context.body:
### The problem

A `statistics` sensor tracking a `binary_sensor` entity will report state as the count over the configured interval, but it only has `icon` and `friendly_name` attributes.

Notably absent is `unit_of_measurement: value` which prevents the count from being graphed unless it's wrapped in a template.

### What is version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

core-2021.6.0.dev0

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

_No response_

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant Core

### Integration causing the issue

statistics

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/statistics

### Example YAML snippet

```yaml
# Example configuration.yaml entry
sensor:
  - platform: simulated
    name: simulated_a
    amplitude: 0.5
    period: 40

  - platform: simulated
    name: simulated_b
    amplitude: 0.5
    period: 25

  - platform: statistics
    name: counted_sim_c_2_min
    entity_id: binary_sensor.simulated_c_binary
    sampling_size: 20
    max_age:
      minutes: 2

template:
  - sensor:
      - name: simulated_c
        state: '{{ states("sensor.simulated_a")|float + states("sensor.simulated_b")|float }}'
        unit_of_measurement: value

  - binary_sensor:
      - name: simulated_c_binary
        state: '{{ states("sensor.simulated_c")|float > 0.0 }}'
```


### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_

I didn't have a problem working with the code structure with my attempted PR so I can't call out any specific spot for clean-up. I was just responding with respect to your comment "Cleaning up with the whole sampling_size and/or max_age mess is on my todo list" - no criticism intended :)

I now see the ambiguity for the "count transitions to on"; feel free to disregard I was just musing (and it's not in scope of this issue anyhow).

As for my use case: I, too, have a motion sensor that will push for a transition to "on" or "off" (I haven't tested the behavior for "unavailable" or another null state to either state). I would like to have a sliding window that measures how much aggregate time it's been in the "on" state as well as how many times it's transitioned to the "on" state to detect ongoing motion. So far I have a proxy for the latter: how many times the sensor has transitioned in a given interval.

This measure of how many times the sensor has transitioned in a given interval is somewhat handy for disambiguating occupancy from something passing by the sensor (to decide when to declare an area unoccupied).

While I made use of the statistics sensor to perform this counting rather than trying to approximate it with some automation (the ability to keep a list of timestamps is crucial) it wasn't exactly what I was looking for. Since I thought I was the only user I figured I'd just make due with tweaking automation events and triggers rather than trying to create some other type of sensor to debounce my motion sensor.

As for the explanation I noted in the other issue (home-assistant/home-assistant.io#17882) that the default behavior will typically count up to 20 and just stay there without much explanation and doesn't have any examples for `binary_sensor` inputs. A bit more explanation with some examples that show the effects of `max_age` and `sampling_size` might be handy. Some examples:

- `max_age` of a 5 minutes but a `sample_size` of 1 to show a statistics sensor that tracks whether a `binary_sensor` changed state in the last 5 minutes.
- `max_age` of 15 minutes and `sample_size` of 100 to show a rolling count of number of transitions over 15 minutes.

Both are handy for PIR motion sensors.

review_comments: @MartinHjelmare I added this for similar parity; while I do find this one more handy it's just republishing an attribute that's part of the definition. If this entity were to move away from YAML like some of the other integrations then it would become handy again but right now it's a bit redundant (with the config). Should I remove this, too?
Good question. Normally we don't add config to state attributes. But sometimes we do add state attributes that are not dynamic if they make automations viable and/or easier to write.
In that case, I think we should leave it because it makes for handy template expressions (especially if you want to determine if you've counted to max value in an interval). Thank you :)

`changes` is not an unit of measurement. The value is counting the state changes but that doesn't mean that we should start adding "what the sensors is doing" as unit of measurement to the values. If giving the sensor a proper name is not enough then one could further specify the unit of measurement (for a badge or a card) with "Customizations".

I think there is a unit of measurement here but we might need to settle on a name. Consider that if you were to derive a rate such as "changes per hour" it would be immediately accurate and meaningful. For it to be unitless doesn't as accurately describe what's being measured.

My initial goal was to have it treated as the number it is rather than a discrete state string. In the process of the review noting that the unit is "changes" I felt added additional some clarity.

If the issue is the specific naming of the unit other meaningful units could be "counts", "state changes", "toggles", "transitions" all have similar meaning.

A search of scholarly papers for "changes per" yields abundant results which I think gives weight to the concept of "changes" as a unit. After some more searching I was also able to find references to SI-prefixed units such as "kilotransitions", "kilocounts", "kcounts", "gigacounts", "gcounts" in papers across various fields.

So if it were changed to use "counts" as a unit it would not only be meaningful it would also be consistent with the chosen unit name for similar measurements.

What do you say to using "counts" here?
I removed this comment; it was inaccurate.

I think I have another option that might apply here and I think it'll address the concern you have with specifying a unit by default. While also solving my issue that a `binary_sensor` won't have a `unit_of_measurement` for this sensor to adopt like it can for a normal `sensor`.

Using a configuration variable to explicitly specify a `unit_of_measurement` (similar to how one would configure a `template` sensor) will solve my problem of keeping a unit bound to my statistics sensor with minimal configuration pain while both avoiding changing the default behavior (making this no longer a breaking change) and avoid having to settle on a specific default unit.

While it is possible to override the missing attribute with customizations or wrapping it in a template sensor I think this is far more elegant and it makes configuration less error prone (it took me a few tries to get it to work as I expected when I was experimenting with it).
We don't want to add config options for unit of measurement. We should just make a decision.
